sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 115 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Not to us, O LORD
study.intro: Psalm 115 belongs to the Egyptian Hallel sung at Passover. It begins by giving all glory to God rather than to His people, then mocks the lifeless idols of the nations, which have mouths, eyes and hands but can do nothing. Three groups are called to trust the LORD as their help and shield, and the psalm closes with promises of blessing and a vow of endless praise.
study.context: Psalm 115 answers a taunt: 'Where is their God?' Israel's God could not be seen as an image, so neighboring peoples mocked. The psalm turns the mockery around: Israel's God is in heaven doing as He pleases, while visible idols are helpless. The call to Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD may have been sung by a leader with the congregation answering. Psalm 135:15-18 repeats the idol passage almost word for word.
study.peopleNote: No author is named. The psalm addresses Israel, the priests of the house of Aaron and all who fear the LORD, a phrase that may include non-Israelites who worshiped Israel's God. Aaron himself is recalled through the priestly line.

verses.title: Glory to Your name
verses.heading: Not to us, but to Your name
verses.meaning: 'Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, because of Your loving devotion, because of Your faithfulness.' The psalm opens by turning the spotlight away from God's people. Any good they have experienced is not their achievement. The credit belongs to God, whose steady covenant love and faithfulness have carried them. The repeated 'not to us' sounds almost urgent, as if pride must be pushed firmly aside.
verses.context: Daniel 9:18 prays not on the basis of Israel's righteousness but because of God's great mercy. Paul writes, 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 1:31).
explore: Glory
Honor, praise and recognition; here the singer insists it belongs to God alone.
Loving devotion
Translating the Hebrew hesed: God's loyal, covenant-keeping love that does not let go.
verses.reflect: Is there something you have been taking credit for that you could give God thanks for instead?
verses.alt: Villagers kneeling in a field at harvest with hands open upward.

verses.title: A mocking question
verses.heading: Where is their God?
verses.meaning: 'Why should the nations say, Where is their God?' Israel's neighbors had visible statues and shrines. Israel worshiped a God who could not be pictured, and when Israel suffered, people sneered that their God must be absent or weak. The psalmist asks God not to let that taunt stand, since it dishonors His name. The question still comes when believers face hardship.
verses.context: Psalm 42:3 and 79:10 record the same mocking question, and Joel 2:17 urges priests to pray that God would not let the nations say it. The taunt was an attack on God's honor.
explore: Nations
The surrounding peoples who did not know or worship Israel's God.
Taunt
A mocking question or insult intended to shame, not to seek an honest answer.
verses.reflect: When others question where God is in your troubles, how do you respond?
verses.alt: Onlookers on a city wall pointing at a small camp below.

verses.title: He does as He pleases
verses.heading: Our God is in heaven
verses.meaning: 'Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases.' Here is the bold answer to the taunt. God is not missing. He is enthroned in heaven, free and sovereign. Nothing limits Him the way idols are limited. He does what He wills, and since He is good and faithful, His free choices can be trusted even when we cannot see them.
verses.context: Psalm 135:6 says the LORD does whatever pleases Him in heaven and on earth. Daniel 4:35 says no one can hold back His hand or ask Him, 'What have You done?'
explore: In heaven
Above and beyond the created world, not confined to any place or image.
As He pleases
According to His own good will, not forced or controlled by anyone.
verses.reflect: How does God's freedom comfort you rather than frighten you?
verses.alt: A clear night sky full of stars over a quiet desert camp.

verses.title: Made by human hands
verses.heading: Silver and gold
verses.meaning: 'Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men.' The idols may be beautiful and valuable, but they have a fatal problem: people made them. A god that a craftsman shapes is smaller than the one who shaped it. Idols today may be money, success or comfort; they are still things we make and then try to depend on.
verses.context: Isaiah 44:9-20 mocks a man who burns half a log for cooking and carves the other half into a god. Acts 17:29 says God is not like gold or silver shaped by human skill.
explore: Idols
Images or objects worshiped as gods; more broadly, anything trusted in place of God.
Made by hands
Crafted by human skill, so dependent on people rather than above them.
verses.reflect: What 'made' thing are you tempted to rely on more than God?
verses.alt: A metalworker's bench with unfinished figurines and tools.

verses.title: Mute and blind
verses.heading: They cannot speak or see
verses.meaning: 'They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see;' The psalmist begins a list that is almost humorous. The statues have all the right features but none of them work. They cannot speak a word of guidance or see the needs of those who pray. Israel's God, by contrast, speaks through His word and sees His people.
verses.contextTitle: A God who speaks and sees
verses.context: Hagar called the LORD 'the God who sees me' (Genesis 16:13). Habakkuk 2:18-19 says it is useless to tell a wooden idol, 'Wake up!', because it has no breath in it.
explore: Mouths that cannot speak
Carved lips that give no word, counsel or answer to those who ask.
Eyes that cannot see
Painted or carved eyes blind to the worshipers standing before them.
verses.reflect: When have you sensed God seeing you or speaking to you?
verses.alt: A carved stone figure covered in dust in an abandoned shrine.

verses.title: Deaf and senseless
verses.heading: Ears that cannot hear
verses.meaning: 'they have ears, but cannot hear; they have noses, but cannot smell;' The list goes on. Idols cannot hear prayers, and they cannot even smell the incense and offerings placed before them. All the worship poured on them goes nowhere. The living God, however, hears every cry, as Psalm 116 will soon say: 'He has heard my voice.'
verses.context: Elijah mocked Baal's prophets, saying perhaps their god was asleep, because no one answered (1 Kings 18:27). Psalm 116:1 rejoices that the LORD hears.
explore: Ears that cannot hear
Shaped ears that receive no prayer, making every request useless.
Noses that cannot smell
Unable to sense offerings and incense; a pointed joke about worthless sacrifices.
verses.reflect: How does it encourage you that your prayers reach a God who truly hears?
verses.alt: Smoke from an offering drifting past an unmoving statue.

verses.title: Powerless limbs
verses.heading: They cannot even clear their throats
verses.meaning: 'they have hands, but cannot feel; they have feet, but cannot walk; they cannot even clear their throats.' The final line is a sharp joke. Idols cannot do the smallest human thing, not even make a sound in the throat. They have to be carried from place to place. The LORD, in contrast, carries His people.
verses.context: Isaiah 46:1-4 contrasts idols that must be loaded onto weary animals with the LORD, who carries His people from birth to old age and will keep carrying them.
explore: Hands that cannot feel
Unable to touch, hold or help anyone who comes to them.
Clear their throats
Make even the smallest sound; idols are utterly silent and lifeless.
verses.reflect: In what ways has God carried you instead of you having to carry Him?
verses.alt: Porters straining to carry a heavy statue on poles.

verses.title: Becoming like them
verses.heading: Those who make them become like them
verses.meaning: 'Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them.' This is the serious point behind the jokes. We become like what we worship. People who trust lifeless things gradually become spiritually deaf, blind and unresponsive. In contrast, those who look to the living God are slowly changed into His likeness.
verses.context: 2 Corinthians 3:18 says believers who behold the Lord's glory are transformed into His image. Jeremiah 2:5 says Israel followed worthless idols and became worthless themselves.
explore: Become like them
Grow to share their emptiness: unseeing, unhearing and unfeeling.
Trust
Rely on something or someone for safety, help, meaning and hope.
verses.reflect: What are you looking at most, and how might it be shaping you?
verses.alt: A villager turning away from a shrine toward an open sunrise.

verses.title: Israel, trust
verses.heading: He is their help and shield
verses.meaning: 'O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.' After exposing idols, the psalm calls the whole nation to trust. The LORD is both help, who comes alongside to act, and shield, who stands between His people and harm. The repeated line in the next verses works like a refrain that the congregation may have sung back.
verses.context: Psalm 33:20 says, 'He is our help and our shield.' Genesis 15:1 has God telling Abram, 'I am your shield, your very great reward.' The same picture runs through the Psalms.
explore: Help
Active aid from someone stronger who steps in when we cannot manage alone.
Shield
Protection held up between a person and attack, like a soldier's shield.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to be your help, and where do you need Him to be your shield?
verses.alt: A soldier's round leather shield leaning against a doorway.

verses.title: Priests, trust
verses.heading: O house of Aaron
verses.meaning: 'O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.' Now the priests are addressed. They served at the altar and led worship, yet they too needed to trust, not in their office or rituals, but in the LORD Himself. Religious leaders are not exempt from the call to depend on God; if anything, they need to model it for everyone else.
verses.context: The house of Aaron were the priests descended from Moses' brother Aaron (Exodus 28:1). Psalm 118:3 also calls them to say, 'His loving devotion endures forever.'
explore: House of Aaron
The priestly family line descended from Aaron, who served at the tabernacle and temple.
Trust
Lean the whole weight of life on God, rather than on position or ritual.
verses.reflect: If you serve or lead in your church or family, how are you trusting God rather than your role?
verses.alt: Priests in plain linen standing by a stone altar at dawn.

verses.title: God-fearers, trust
verses.heading: You who fear the LORD
verses.meaning: 'You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.' The third group is wider: all who revere God. This may include foreigners who came to worship Israel's God, like Ruth. The circle of invitation grows outward. Anyone who fears the LORD is welcome to trust Him and find Him a help and a shield.
verses.context: In Acts the 'God-fearers' were Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God, such as Cornelius (Acts 10:2). Ruth the Moabite chose Israel's God as her own (Ruth 1:16).
explore: Fear the LORD
Honor and revere God in a way that leads to trust and obedience.
God-fearers
A later name for non-Israelites who worshiped the God of Israel.
verses.reflect: How does it encourage you that God's invitation reaches beyond any single group?
verses.alt: A traveler from far away joining a gathered crowd at a gate.

verses.title: The LORD remembers us
verses.heading: He will bless us
verses.meaning: 'The LORD is mindful of us; He will bless us. He will bless the house of Israel; He will bless the house of Aaron;' The refrain turns to promise. God has not forgotten His people. He remembers them and will bless them. Then the same groups from verses 9 and 10 are named again, now not as those called to trust, but as those who will be blessed.
verses.context: In Genesis 8:1 God remembered Noah, and in Exodus 2:24 He remembered His covenant with Abraham. To be remembered by God means He acts on our behalf.
explore: Mindful
Keeping someone in mind with care, ready to act for them.
Bless
To give good gifts, life and favor; to cause someone to flourish.
verses.reflect: What does it mean to you that God keeps you in mind?
verses.alt: A mother looking up from work to watch children play nearby.

verses.title: Small and great alike
verses.heading: Those who fear the LORD
verses.meaning: 'He will bless those who fear the LORD—small and great alike.' God's blessing is not reserved for the important. Children and elders, poor and rich, the unknown and the famous are blessed together. No one is too insignificant for His attention, and no one is too great to need it. Every worshiper stands on the same level ground before God.
verses.context: Revelation 11:18 and 19:5 speak of God's servants 'small and great'. Acts 10:34 says God shows no favoritism, and Job 34:19 says He made rich and poor alike.
explore: Small and great
People of every rank, age and importance, from children to rulers.
Alike
Equally and together, without one group being favored over another.
verses.reflect: Do you ever feel too small for God to notice? What does this verse say to that?
verses.alt: A child and an old man walking side by side to a gathering.

verses.title: Increase for families
verses.heading: You and your children
verses.meaning: 'May the LORD give you increase, both you and your children.' The psalm now speaks a blessing over the congregation, perhaps from the priests. It asks God to multiply them and their families. In a world where families and flocks could dwindle through war and famine, growth was a precious gift from God.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 1:11 prays that God would multiply Israel a thousand times. Numbers 6:24-26 records the priestly blessing Aaron's sons spoke over Israel.
explore: Increase
Growth in number, strength and fruitfulness, given by God.
Children
The next generation, who share in the blessing of their parents' faith.
verses.reflect: Whose children or family could you pray God's blessing over today?
verses.alt: A large family seated together outside a stone house at evening.

verses.title: Blessed by the Maker
verses.heading: Maker of heaven and earth
verses.meaning: 'May you be blessed by the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' The blessing has unlimited backing. It comes from the One who made everything, not from a carved idol. Since He created heaven and earth, nothing in them is beyond His power to give or to protect. That makes this blessing far stronger than any wish people could speak on their own.
verses.context: Psalm 121:2 says, 'My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.' Psalm 134:3 ends the Songs of Ascents with the same blessing.
explore: Maker
The Creator who formed everything that exists, seen and unseen.
Heaven and earth
The whole universe, the sky above and the land below and all they contain.
verses.reflect: How does knowing the Creator Himself blesses you change your view of your needs?
verses.alt: Mountains and sky meeting at the horizon above a green valley.

verses.title: Earth entrusted to us
verses.heading: Given to mankind
verses.meaning: 'The highest heavens belong to the LORD, but the earth He has given to mankind.' God owns the heavens, and He has entrusted the earth to people. This echoes Genesis 1, where humans are given care of creation. The earth is a gift and a responsibility: we live on it as stewards under God, not as its owners.
verses.context: Genesis 1:28 gives humanity rule over the earth, and Genesis 2:15 places Adam in the garden 'to cultivate and keep it.' Psalm 24:1 reminds that the earth is still the LORD's.
explore: Highest heavens
The heavens above the heavens, God's own realm beyond the sky.
Given to mankind
Entrusted to human care and work, as stewards accountable to God.
verses.reflect: How could you care for the part of the earth God has entrusted to you?
verses.alt: A farmer tending young plants in a terraced garden.

verses.title: The silence of the grave
verses.heading: Not the dead who praise
verses.meaning: 'It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence.' The psalmist reflects that the grave falls silent. Life is the time to praise God aloud among the living. Old Testament believers had only glimpses of resurrection, so this verse urges them to use the breath they have now. The New Testament adds the hope that death will not have the last word.
verses.context: Psalm 6:5 and Isaiah 38:18-19 make the same point. Later Scripture reveals a fuller hope: 1 Corinthians 15:55 asks, 'Where, O death, is your victory?'
explore: Descend into silence
Go down to the grave, pictured as a place where voices are no longer heard.
The dead
Those whose earthly life has ended and who no longer join the living congregation.
verses.reflect: How could you make the most of today as a time to praise God?
verses.alt: An empty stone bench under an olive tree at dusk.

verses.title: We will bless Him
verses.heading: Now and forevermore
verses.meaning: 'But it is we who will bless the LORD, both now and forevermore. Hallelujah!' The living congregation answers: we will praise. The psalm that began with 'not to us' ends with 'it is we' — not claiming glory, but gladly giving it. The praise begins now and stretches forever, ending with a final 'Hallelujah.'
verses.contextTitle: From 'not to us' to 'we will bless'
verses.context: Psalm 113:2 had the same phrase, 'now and forevermore.' The pattern of humble beginnings and joyful endings runs through the Hallel psalms sung at Passover.
explore: We will bless
A determined promise from the living to keep praising God.
Hallelujah
Hebrew for 'Praise the LORD', a call that ends many psalms of praise.
verses.reflect: What is one specific way you will bless the LORD out loud today?
verses.alt: A crowd raising hands together in an open courtyard at sunrise.
